part_title: Enterprise Retrieval, Citations and Access Permissions
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 1 through 4 individually in source order, verifying visible labels, workflows, examples, access-control boundaries, and service distinctions; rewritten as balanced-length teaching narration.

scenes.title: Amazon Q Business
scenes.narration: Begin with the flow across the top of this slide. Amazon Q Business helps employees ask questions using information held by their own organization. Company documents live in sources such as Amazon S3 and SharePoint. Data connectors ingest, split and index that content so it can be searched by meaning. The yellow panel shows permission-aware retrieval: Q Business should return only content the signed-in employee is authorized to access. Finally, the right-hand panel generates an answer with links back to the source documents. Look at the worked example below. An employee asks what the team discussed in the project meeting. The illustrative answer mentions launch risks and owners, with meeting notes cited as the source. Citations allow the employee to inspect where that statement came from. The exam comparison in the lower right distinguishes two assistants. Choose Amazon Q Business for questions across company policies and documents. Choose Amazon Q Developer for coding, AWS architecture guidance and development tasks. Q Business does not give everyone access to every company document: the security of the original sources and the identity configuration still matter.

scenes.title: A grounded answer from company documents
scenes.narration: This diagram follows a more detailed, permission-aware answer. Start with the three documents on the left: an HR handbook available to the HR team, employee policies available to all employees, and a benefits FAQ. These ACL labels mean access-control lists: rules describing who can read particular content. The connectors bring documents from SharePoint, Google Drive and S3 into the Q Business search index, including metadata about permissions. When a signed-in employee asks, 'What is our leave policy?', Q Business must filter the indexed content before it generates an answer. The lower middle panel explicitly marks the restricted HR handbook as inaccessible. Employee policies and the benefits FAQ remain eligible. The retrieved example says employees receive twenty days of annual leave, and the final answer cites that employee policy. Notice the yellow note: this is illustrative text, not an actual company leave policy. The important lesson is the order of operations. Authentication identifies the user; source permissions constrain which passages may be retrieved; the model answers using authorized evidence. A citation is useful for checking accuracy, but permission checks are essential even when a document looks relevant.

scenes.title: Connectors versus plugins
scenes.narration: This slide compares connectors with plugins, two different integration jobs. On the top left, Amazon S3 contains policies and reports while SharePoint contains intranet files and wikis. Connectors ingest and index that content so Q Business can retrieve passages and provide citations. In the upper right, the separate authorized-plugin branch calls an external API, shown here with Jira. That branch can perform a read or write action rather than merely searching documents. Walk through the example in the middle: first an employee asks what the work-from-home policy says, so Q Business retrieves a grounded answer. Then the employee asks to create a Jira issue to review the policy. A configured plugin calls Jira to create a task, subject to appropriate permissions and confirmation for the write. The distinction at the bottom is the exam decision rule: connector equals search and grounded retrieval; plugin equals an authorized external action. A plugin does not automatically index all the documents in Jira, and a connector does not itself create a Jira issue. Treat API credentials, user identity and allowed actions as real security boundaries, not just settings in a prompt.

scenes.title: Identity and source permissions
scenes.narration: Follow the five boxes from left to right. The employee signs in using company credentials, IAM Identity Center authenticates that workforce identity, and the Amazon Q Business web application receives the authenticated user context. It can search connected documents from services such as SharePoint, Confluence and S3, but only where access is allowed. The final answer is based on accessible company content. Now look at the administrator setup below. First connect the workforce directory to IAM Identity Center, then configure the Q Business application, and finally preserve and enforce document permissions in the connected sources. The two examples illustrate why identity and authorization are different. An HR employee who can read HR documents may receive a response about parental leave policy. An Engineering employee without those rights should not receive the confidential HR passage merely because they successfully signed in. Authentication answers 'Who are you?' while authorization answers 'Which information can you access?' On the exam, selecting IAM Identity Center for workforce sign-in is correct, but it does not replace source-document permission enforcement.
